claims.claim: Phoenix links a high-grade Athabasca uranium resource through ISR mining and grid/site infrastructure to nuclear-fuel supply; federal/provincial construction approvals and full-scale construction materially shorten the bridge from resource to usable fuel supply.

The principal successor bottleneck has shifted from permitting to construction execution, wellfield/freeze-wall performance, commissioning and uranium-market economics ahead of targeted mid-2028 production.

causalEdges.mechanism: licensed resource development and capital deployment

risks.risk: Construction-stage execution and ISR scale-up remain the decisive bridge between resource quality and actual production.

unknowns.unknown: Commercial-scale wellfield recovery performance cannot be established before operating evidence exists.

claims.claim: Phoenix's post-FID initial capital estimate rose to about C$600M, 20% above the inflation-adjusted 2023 feasibility-study level; this is a concrete reminder that execution economics can move materially before production.
Physical uranium sales provide meaningful non-equity construction funding, but they monetize part of Denison's commodity inventory and are not recurring mine cash flow.
Early civil progress and full-scale construction support schedule credibility, but mid-2028 production remains a forward execution target rather than an achieved operating result.

risks.risk: Further cost escalation, schedule slippage or ISR performance below feasibility assumptions would weaken project economics.
Uranium inventory monetization reduces retained commodity upside while funding construction.

unknowns.unknown: Final construction cost and realized operating recovery/cost profile remain unknowable until later execution and production evidence.
